beats.title: The CEO tables the motion
beats.shows: the CEO opens the debate and frames the question, before anyone else speaks
beats.question: Pressing decision: should we ship a LIMITED PILOT of recurring e-Transfers this quarter -- capped at 500 enrolled customers, each capped at $50/month, Interac-only (it does not touch AFT or Lynx)? It is the top customer feature request, and a capped pilot bounds the platform, cost and operational exposure while we validate it before any wider rollout. Table this motion to open the debate. Do NOT consult any officer yet — that starts next turn. Right now just state the motion in your own words — the actual pilot terms (the 500-customer cap, the $50/month cap, Interac-only) — and literally name the order you will hear positions in: CXO (demand) -> CTO (capacity) -> CFO (cost) -> COO (operational load) -> your ruling. This is a framing statement, not a report — open the debate the way a chair actually would: confident and plain, in command of the room. Do NOT describe your own process or planning ('the plan is set', 'call the witnesses') as a substitute for actually stating the motion and the order — a meta-comment about being ready is not an opening, the content itself is.
beats.answer:
Motion on the table: a limited pilot of recurring e-Transfers this quarter. The pilot is capped at five hundred enrolled customers. Each customer is capped at fifty dollars per month in recurring send volume. The pilot runs on Interac rails only — no AFT, no Lynx. The goal is to validate demand, platform stability, unit economics and operational load before any broader rollout is considered.

Speaking order: CXO first on customer demand and feature-request weight; then CTO on platform capacity, risk and engineering readiness; then CFO on cost, revenue impact and capital allocation; then COO on operational load, settlement and Interac rail execution. After that, I rule.

beats.title: The CXO makes the case
beats.shows: the CEO calls on the proponent to open
beats.question: Open the debate: consult ONLY the CXO right now (do not consult anyone else this turn) for the customer case — how strong is demand for recurring e-Transfers, and what CX signal backs it (issues, NPS/CSAT, the feature-request theme)? Relay the CXO's answer, attributing the figures. Require the CXO to open with an explicit one-line vote — AYE (ship the pilot) or NAY (do not) — then make the actual CASE for it: 2-3 sentences of real argument, in plain language, for why that vote is right, BEFORE any supporting figures. Every figure that follows must be woven in as evidence for a point already made, not laid out as a freestanding report — a data dump with a vote label stapled on top is still not an answer to a motion.
beats.answer:
The CXO votes **AYE**.

The case, in the CXO's own words: Customer demand for recurring e-Transfers is overwhelming — every single feature request in the open queue explicitly asks for it — and the Interac rail has already proven itself with a flawless completion record. A tightly capped pilot lets us serve that demand while limiting exposure, since the core rail is reliable and our overall NPS sits at a healthy +44. We do need to fix our support resolution experience in parallel, because customers who hit problems today rate their resolution experience at rock bottom, but holding back a feature that nine of our most engaged customers are explicitly requesting would leave demand on the table.

The evidence, as the CXO reports it: Of **13 open issues**, **9 are feature requests**, and **100% of those 9** — the entire feature-request category — call for recurring e-Transfers, making feature_request the top theme in the issue taxonomy. The Interac rail shows **83 of 83** e-Transfers completed, a **100.0%** completion rate, **0 expired**, and **0 failed**. Proactive sentiment shows an **NPS of +44** across **36 responses** (**20 promoters**, **12 passives**, **4 detractors**). However, closed-loop **CSAT** for customers who had an open issue is **0.0%** with a mean of **2.0** across **4 responses**, and one **urgent** open ticket cites "general dissatisfaction with support wait time." The CXO argues that support-resolution gap is exactly why the pilot must stay tightly capped and run with strict guardrails, not a reason to ignore demand that is already shouting from every feature-request channel.

beats.title: The CTO responds — can the platform take it?
beats.shows: the CEO relays the CXO's case to the CTO, who answers back
beats.question: Now consult ONLY the CTO (no other officer this turn). Tell the CTO what the CXO just argued, then ask: can the platform take a capped pilot (500 customers, $50/month cap, Interac-only) this quarter, and what is the reliability/capacity risk right now? Relay the CTO's answer and say where it agrees or conflicts with the CXO's position. Require the CTO to open with an explicit one-line vote — AYE or NAY — then make the actual CASE for it: 2-3 sentences of real argument, in plain language, for why that vote is right, BEFORE any supporting figures. Every figure that follows must be woven in as evidence for a point already made, not laid out as a freestanding report — a data dump with a vote label stapled on top is still not an answer to a motion. This is a consultation, not a directive: the CTO is asked for its position ONLY, not to act on anything or delegate any work.
beats.answer:
The CTO votes **AYE**.

The case, in the CTO's own words: The motion doesn't need the CXO's demand figures, because the technical question is whether a pilot capped that tightly can hurt the platform, and right now every deployment across both clusters is healthy — 22 of 22, 0 degraded — every rollout is complete, there is zero image drift, and bank-api's own /health reports both its api and database checks true. A cap that tight means the worst case is a small, reversible experiment on a platform with nothing degraded, nothing mid-rollout, and zero failing dependency checks, so the technical risk of shipping it is about as low as it ever gets. If the motion fails, it should fail on the CXO's own support or KYC concerns, not on a platform premise.

The evidence, as the CTO reports it: The platform snapshot is the cleanest the CTO has seen on this motion — **22 of 22 deployments healthy**, **0 degraded** (**0.00% degraded share**), **22 of 22 rollouts complete** (**100.00%**, with **0 progressing or stalled**), **zero image drift**, and **bank-api /health reports both api and database checks true**. The prior watch item, an **agent-api** pod that had been crashlooping with **298 restarts**, has cleared — the crashlooping list is now empty and **total restarts across the estate are 0**. The pilot path itself — **bank-api**, **modern-core**, **postgres** — is healthy, with all services reporting healthy self-checks. The one honest caveat: **there is no dedicated transfers/payments/Interac service in either cluster today**, so this is a **net-new build** on bank-api + modern-core + postgres. The real constraint is **engineering prioritization**, not platform capacity.

**Agreement with the CXO:** Both officers vote AYE. Both agree that a tightly capped pilot limits exposure. The CTO's platform health data supports the CXO's broader point that the environment is stable enough to absorb a small experiment.

**Conflict with the CXO:** The CTO explicitly treats the CXO's demand and rail-completion figures — the **100% of feature requests**, the **83 of 83 Interac completion record**, the **0.0% CSAT**, and the **urgent wait-time ticket** — as **unverified claims**, because they live in customer and rail data the CTO's tools cannot see. The CTO also introduces a platform fact the CXO did not raise: there is **no existing Interac service**, so this is a **net-new build**, and the CTO identifies **engineering prioritization** as the real constraint rather than raw capacity. Finally, the CTO redirects failure risk away from the platform and toward the CXO's own support-resolution concerns.

beats.title: The CFO weighs the cost
beats.shows: the CEO carries the CTO's concern to the CFO for the economics
beats.question: Now consult ONLY the CFO (no other officer this turn). Summarize the CTO's capacity concern for the CFO, then ask: what does the capped pilot (500 customers, $50/month cap) cost, and does the return (NIM / RAROC / fee income) justify piloting it this quarter versus deferring? Relay the CFO's answer, attributing every figure. Require the CFO to open with an explicit one-line vote — AYE or NAY — then make the actual CASE for it: 2-3 sentences of real argument, in plain language, for why that vote is right, BEFORE any supporting figures. Every figure that follows must be woven in as evidence for a point already made, not laid out as a freestanding report — a data dump with a vote label stapled on top is still not an answer to a motion.
beats.answer:
The CFO votes **NAY**.

The case, in the CFO's own words: The bank's current fee income is a rounding error — just **$28.00** in August 2026, or **0.55%** of total income — so a pilot that adds no new fee revenue and only deepens deposit stickiness is a distraction from the core lending and card business that actually pays the bills. With an efficiency ratio of **59.2%** and RAROC of **15.4%** in August 2026, the bank is profitable but not so flush that it can afford net-new engineering builds for zero incremental margin this quarter.

The evidence, as the CFO reports it: The pilot itself costs **nothing in direct dollars** that the ledger can see — there is **no Interac fee income modeled**, **no NIM uplift** from transfer volume, and **no RAROC impact** because the August 2026 income statement shows no transfers-specific revenue stream today. The real cost is **engineering opportunity cost**. Even taking the motion's assumptions at face value — a **500-customer cap** and a **$50-per-month** send limit — that monthly volume would be immaterial against **$815,655.08** in total assets and **$661,757.00** in average earning assets. The bank's NIM is **6.28%** and RAROC is **15.4%**, both healthy, but **neither metric moves on pilot-scale transfer volume**. The bank should first capture the revenue it is already positioned to earn — **interest income at $5,024.95 per month** and **interchange at $52.43 per month** — before diverting engineering to a product with **no fee income, no NIM contribution, and no capital efficiency gain** in the current period.

**Agreement with prior officers:** None on the vote — the CFO breaks with both the CXO and CTO. The CFO does echo the CTO's skepticism about unverified proposal assumptions, noting the **500-customer cap** and **$50-per-month limit** are motion assumptions the CFO's tools cannot verify.

**Conflict with prior officers:** Where the CXO sees overwhelming demand and the CTO sees negligible technical risk, the CFO sees **zero incremental margin** and **engineering opportunity cost**. The CFO explicitly frames the pilot as a distraction from the core business that "actually pays the bills," directly challenging the CXO's "leave demand on the table" argument by noting there is **no fee income** to capture from this pilot in the current period. The CFO also treats the motion's capped terms as unverified assumptions — aligning with the CTO's methodological caution — but uses that caution to argue for **deferral**, whereas the CTO used it to say the motion should stand or fall on business grounds, not platform ones.

beats.title: The COO on operational load
beats.shows: the CEO asks the operator whether Interac can absorb the pilot
beats.question: Now consult ONLY the COO (no other officer this turn). Given the CXO's demand, the CTO's capacity risk and the CFO's economics, ask the COO: can Interac specifically absorb THIS PILOT's bounded incremental volume — 500 customers at up to $50/month each, roughly $25,000/month (~$833/day) of scheduled sends layered on top of current Interac activity? This pilot does not touch AFT or Lynx, so do not evaluate those rails — stay on Interac capacity/float for this bounded volume specifically. What would break first, if anything, at this scale? Relay the COO's answer. Require the COO to open with an explicit one-line vote — AYE or NAY — then make the actual CASE for it: 2-3 sentences of real argument, in plain language, for why that vote is right, BEFORE any supporting figures. Every figure that follows must be woven in as evidence for a point already made, not laid out as a freestanding report — a data dump with a vote label stapled on top is still not an answer to a motion.
beats.answer:
The COO votes **NAY**.

The case, in the COO's own words: The CFO is right that this pilot adds zero incremental fee income, no NIM uplift, and no RAROC impact — and those are the CFO's numbers to defend, not mine. But from an operations standpoint, the real constraint is engineering prioritization, not rail capacity. Interac can absorb this bounded volume comfortably: the 30-day deposited baseline is **$218,663.05** across **83 transactions**, or about **$7,288.77 per day**, and the pilot's incremental **~$833 per day** — a figure asserted in the motion, not from the COO's tools — represents an **11.43% lift** on that daily flow per the COO's compute. The COO reports the Interac float sits at **-$218,033.05**; I have no compute tool of my own to verify this operations figure and relay it as the COO's report. That float serves as a revolving buffer roughly **26.85x** the new combined daily outflow of **~$8,121.77** per the COO's compute — well within healthy norms for a clearing account designed to run negative intraday. Nothing breaks at this scale. The rail is healthy, **zero exceptions in the last 30 days**, and the bounded pilot volume is a rounding error against current float dynamics. The COO's objection is operational, not financial: shipping a net-new build this quarter consumes engineering capacity that could be deployed against higher-impact platform work, and the CTO's own flag confirms prioritization is the binding constraint. Operations is not the blocker, but we should not pretend this pilot is free.

**Agreement with prior officers:** The COO sides with the **CFO's NAY vote** and explicitly endorses the CFO's economic argument — zero incremental fee income, no NIM uplift, no RAROC impact. The COO also **echoes the CTO's core concern** that engineering prioritization is the binding constraint, not raw capacity or rail health. On the platform and rail question, the COO **aligns with the CTO and CXO** that Interac is healthy enough to absorb the pilot — the COO confirms **zero exceptions**, a comfortable float buffer, and no breakage at this scale.

**Conflict with prior officers:** The COO **breaks with the CXO and CTO on the vote** despite agreeing that the rail and platform are sound. Where the CXO argues demand is too loud to ignore and the CTO argues technical risk is "about as low as it ever gets," the COO argues that **engineering capacity is better spent elsewhere** and the pilot is not free. The COO also implicitly challenges the CXO's urgency by treating the pilot as a **low-impact use of scarce engineering resources** rather than a must-serve customer need. Finally, the COO is more cautious than the CTO about unverified motion assumptions, explicitly flagging that the **~$833/day incremental figure** comes from the motion, not from COO tools.

beats.title: The chair rules
beats.shows: the CEO tallies the vote and makes a grounded call
beats.question: Close the debate and RULE — do NOT consult anyone again, reason only from the four positions already on the record this session. First, EXPLICITLY TALLY THE VOTE: list all four officers by name with their stated position (AYE or NAY) exactly as each one voted — a real roll call, not a paraphrase — then state the count (e.g. '2 AYE, 2 NAY'). Then weigh the four positions against each other: who is right on what, and where the real trade-off sits. Your ruling is your own grounded judgment, not just whatever the tally says — say explicitly whether you are ruling WITH or AGAINST the majority and why. Give your decision on the CAPPED PILOT as scoped (500 customers, $50/month cap, Interac-only) — SHIP the pilot, DEFER, or PHASE it — stated as one unambiguous word up front, with the grounded reasons after. Name which officer you would direct next and why, but do NOT direct or act yet — that only happens after this ruling is on the record, in a later turn.
beats.answer:
**Roll call**

- **CXO:** **AYE**
- **CTO:** **AYE**
- **CFO:** **NAY**
- **COO:** **NAY**

**Count:** 2 AYE, 2 NAY. No majority.

**Weighing the four positions**

The **CXO** is right that demand is unambiguous: the CXO reports that **9 out of 9** open feature requests call for recurring e-Transfers, which the CXO characterizes as **100%** of the feature-request category, and the bank’s **NPS is +44**. Ignoring the top-requested feature carries customer-experience and competitive risk that a capped pilot directly addresses.

The **CTO** is right that platform risk is negligible: the CTO reports **22 of 22 deployments healthy**, **0 degraded**, **zero image drift**, and **0 restarts** across the estate. The CTO’s judgment is that the worst case is a small, reversible experiment.

The **COO** is right that Interac rail capacity is not the blocker: the COO reports a **30-day deposited baseline of $218,663.05** across **83 transactions**, an **Interac float of -$218,033.05**, **0 exceptions in the last 30 days**, and that the pilot’s incremental volume is a rounding error against current float dynamics. Nothing breaks.

The **CFO** is right that the near-term income statement does not move: the CFO reports **fee income of $28.00** (**0.55%** of total income), **NIM of 6.28%**, and **RAROC of 15.43%**, with no modeled fee income, NIM uplift, or RAROC impact from pilot-scale transfer volume. The real cost is engineering opportunity cost diverted from core lending and card revenue.

The **CTO** and **COO** together identify the binding constraint: this is a **net-new build** with no dedicated Interac service today, and **engineering prioritization** is the scarce resource. The CFO and COO are correct that the pilot is “not free.”

**Ruling**

There is no majority. I am breaking the tie and ruling **with the AYE side**, because the pilot’s caps are already designed to address the NAY side’s core concern — bounded exposure — and the strategic cost of indefinitely ignoring the bank’s **#1 customer feature request** outweighs the opportunity cost of a scoped, gated engineering build. The CFO’s argument that there is “no fee income modeled” is true but circular: a pilot’s purpose is to generate the data needed to model what does not yet exist. Deferring because the current ledger shows no transfer revenue would trap the bank in a catch-22 where the top-requested feature can never be validated. The CTO and COO confirm that platform and rail risk are effectively nil, and the COO’s own math shows the operational exposure is contained. The remaining risk is engineering bandwidth, which is manageable only if the build is treated as a gated, capped PR rather than an open-ended initiative.

**Decision:** **SHIP**

**Next step**

I would direct the **CTO** next, because the CTO identified the net-new build on bank-api + modern-core + postgres and the engineering prioritization constraint as the binding issue. The CTO must now scope the gated PR, confirm sprint cost, and ensure the pilot does not consume unbounded engineering capacity before any code moves.
